newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK people confident in future but fear corruption.
newsitem.headline: HK people confident in future but fear corruption.

text.p: Most Hong Kong people are optimistic about the shift to Chinese rule this year, but their optimism is fragile and they fear corruption will grow after the sovereignty change, a detailed survey showed on Thursday.
The survey was conducted by Hong Kong Baptist University's "Transition Project", which has been tracking the shifts in attitudes in the years before the handover.

The survey found 62 percent of 546 respondents were optimistic about Hong Kong's transfer to China in 110 days' time after more than 150 years as a British colony, although their longer-term political confidence was weaker.
Their optimism assumed continued prosperity, and, if the economy faltered, that optimism would waver, project director Michael DeGolyer said.
"People are already politically pessimistic. They are already politically sensitive. It is the economic performance that holds them together," DeGolyer said.
When respondents were asked how they felt about Hong Kong's future political performance, only 40 percent said they were confident, and 23 percent said they lacked confidence.
If there were events in Hong Kong of a political nature that affected people's freedom and way of life, more than 40 percent of the respondents said they would leave.

Fifty percent believed that Hong Kong people did not care about politics, while 38 percent believed they cared, which DeGolyer said disproved claims by post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa that Hong Kong people were apolitical.
Tung said in a television interview two weeks ago that bread-and butter issues were of more concern to the territory's 6.4 million people than political liberties.
"We have a spiralling cost of housing...mismatch of skills, education...these are the real problems which people care about," Tung said.
More than half of the respondents in the latest survey said corruption would be more common among government officials after China takes over the British colony on July 1.
When asked whether corruption was common among current colonial government officials, 55 percent said no.
Apart from weak confidence in receiving a clean post-colonial government, the public was more dissatisfied with Tung than with departing British Governor Chris Patten.
More than 60 percent said they were happy with Patten's performance, while Tung scored only 53 percent.
DeGolyer said that was probably due to Tung's support for China's plan to roll back civil liberties after the handover.
The poll found 52 percent of the respondents opposed Beijing's plan and only 20 percent supported it.
